blocks.prompt: A Bill Full of Air
blocks.text: A toucan's bill is longer than the rest of its head. It looks like it should tip the bird right over. It does not. Inside the bill there is no heavy bone. There is a web of thin struts with air in all the gaps, like the inside of a sponge. That makes the bill light and strong at the same time. The toucan uses it to reach fruit on branches too thin to stand on. It grabs the fruit with the tip, tosses its head back, and swallows. Toucans live in the warm forests of Central America and South America. When the day gets hot, the bird lets extra heat run out through its big bill.

blocks.prompt: The Bill That Is Mostly Air
blocks.text: A toco toucan is about as long as your arm, and almost a third of that length is bill. A bill that size should weigh the bird down. It weighs almost nothing. Look inside one and you find no solid bone. You find a hard outer shell of keratin, the same stuff your fingernails are made of, and under it a maze of thin bony struts with air in every gap. The whole thing is mostly empty space. The toucan needs the reach. Fruit grows at the ends of branches, out where a heavy bird cannot perch. So the toucan sits on a strong branch, stretches that long bill out, plucks the fruit with the tip, then flips its head back and lets the fruit drop down its throat. The edges of the bill are jagged like a small saw, which helps it hold on to slippery fruit. At night the toucan does something odd. It turns its head around, lays the bill flat along its back, and folds its tail up over the top. A sleeping toucan is a ball of feathers with no bill in sight.

blocks.prompt: Toucans Keep Their Cool
blocks.text: For a long time nobody could say what the toucan's bill was actually for. Charles Darwin looked at the bright colors and guessed it helped the bird attract a mate. Other naturalists said it was a weapon, or a tool for peeling tough fruit, or a mask to bluff rivals away from a nest hole. Every guess had a problem. The bill is far too fragile to win a fight, and far too loud to be a good disguise. In 2009 a team of scientists pointed a thermal camera at some toco toucans. A thermal camera does not see color. It sees heat, and it draws hot things bright. On the screen the toucan's body glowed dim while its bill glowed brilliant, and the brightness kept changing. The birds were opening and closing the blood vessels inside the bill. When they needed to cool down, hot blood flooded in and the heat poured off the surface. When they wanted to keep their warmth, they shut the flow off and the bill went dark, sometimes in only a few minutes. Birds cannot sweat. The toucan solves that with a radiator it wears on its face, and it can turn the radiator up or down whenever it likes. At night it tucks the bill under its feathers and switches the whole thing off. Other animals have found the same answer. Elephants do it with their ears. Jackrabbits do it with theirs. A bare, blood-rich surface you can flood or drain is a useful thing to own in a hot country, and the toucan happens to carry one on the front of its head.

notes: Ramphastos toco, the largest toucan
Bill: keratin shell over a lattice of struts and air
Thermal radiator, proven with heat cameras in 2009
Tongue is long, gray, and frayed like a feather
Swallows fruit whole and scatters the seeds

blocks.prompt: Everything the Bill Is For
blocks.text: Ask what a toucan's bill is for and you get several answers, all of them partly right. Start with reach. Toucans eat fruit, and fruit hangs at the ends of thin branches, out where a bird weighing a pound and a half cannot perch. Sitting on a solid limb and stretching out eight inches of bill solves that problem without asking the twig to hold anything. The tip closes on the fruit, the head snaps back, and the fruit drops down the throat. The edges of the bill are serrated, which grips slippery skins, and a long gray tongue, frayed along both sides like a feather, works the food backward. Then temperature. Birds cannot sweat. In 2009 researchers filmed toco toucans with a thermal camera, which draws heat as brightness, and watched the birds flood the bill with warm blood when they needed to dump heat, then shut the flow down when they did not. The bill is a radiator with a tap on it. At night, with the bill laid along the back and the tail folded over the top, the tap closes and the bird keeps its warmth. Then the forest itself. A toucan swallows fruit whole and passes the seeds later, well away from the tree that made them. Big seeds need big-billed birds to move them. In Brazilian forest fragments where the large toucans have vanished, researchers found palms producing measurably smaller seeds, generation after generation, because nothing was left that could carry the big ones anywhere. Remove the bird and the trees change shape. And then there is what the bill is not. It is not much of a weapon. It is a keratin shell over a lattice of struts and air, strong for its weight and light for its size, but hollow, and nobody would pick it for a fight. Toucans are not much for flying either, with short rounded wings that suit a flap-and-glide hop from tree to tree rather than a long crossing. The most spectacular tool on the bird turns out to be a fruit picker, a radiator, and a seed truck. Not a sword.

6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Toucan and Its Impossible Bill

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Ramphastos toco: the largest of about 40 toucan species
Largest bill relative to body size of any living bird
Keratin plates over an air-filled bony lattice
Tattersall et al., 2009: a controllable vascular radiator
Galetti et al., 2013: lose the toucans, palm seeds shrink
Order Piciformes, the same branch as woodpeckers

blocks.prompt: Three Answers to One Question
blocks.text: The toco toucan carries the largest bill, relative to body size, of any bird alive. On an animal roughly two feet long, the bill runs about eight inches: a third of the bird, bright orange, tipped with a black spot, and impossible to ignore. For most of the history of biology, nobody could say what it was for. The guesses came quickly and failed slowly. Charles Darwin, looking at the color, proposed sexual display. Other naturalists argued for a weapon, or a fruit-peeling tool, or a threat mask to bluff rivals away from a nest hole. Each explanation ran into the same wall. The bill is not built like a tool that does any of those jobs well, because it is barely built at all. The outside is keratin, the material of your fingernails, laid down in overlapping plates. The inside is a lattice of thin bony struts around pockets of air, closer to a sponge or a bicycle helmet than to bone. The bill is a third of the bird's length and roughly a thirtieth of its weight. Engineers study it for exactly that ratio: enormous, rigid, and nearly weightless. The main answer arrived in 2009. Glenn Tattersall and his colleagues placed toco toucans in a temperature-controlled chamber and watched them through a thermal camera, which renders heat as brightness. What they saw was a bill that switched on and off. When the birds needed to shed heat, blood vessels near the surface opened and the bill blazed white on the screen. When the birds needed to conserve heat, those vessels clamped down and the bill went dark, sometimes within minutes. Birds cannot sweat. The toucan instead carries a controllable radiator on its face, one it can flood or drain at will. At the end of the day it turns its head backward, lays the bill along its spine, folds its tail up over the top, and sleeps as a ball of feathers with the radiator switched off and buried. That does not mean the bill is only a radiator. Toucans eat fruit that hangs at the tips of thin branches, out where a bird of their weight cannot perch. Sitting on a solid limb and reaching eight inches solves that problem elegantly. The serrated edges grip slick fruit skins, and a long gray tongue, frayed along both sides like a feather, moves food back toward the throat. The bird swallows fruit whole and drops the seeds elsewhere, which makes it one of the forest's delivery systems. Large seeds need large-gaped birds. When Mauro Galetti's team surveyed Brazilian forest fragments that had lost their big toucans, they found palms there producing measurably smaller seeds, generation after generation, because only the small ones were still being carried anywhere. Remove the bird and the trees change shape. So the bill is a reaching tool, a radiator, and a seed truck, and it is worth asking why that took so long to work out. Each early guess assumed a single purpose, because a structure that dramatic seemed to demand one dramatic reason. Evolution does not work that way. It builds compromises, and a good compromise usually does several jobs adequately rather than one job perfectly. The toucan's bill was never a mystery waiting for its answer. It was a mystery with three answers at once, and biology kept looking for one.
